source.title: Nine open problems on conjunctive and Boolean grammars

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a language that can be recognized by a deterministic linear bounded automaton using O(n^2) time on inputs of length n, but cannot be generated by any Boolean grammar? Here a Boolean grammar is a formal grammar extending context-free grammars with implicit disjunction, explicit conjunction in rule bodies, and explicit negation.

Do conjunctive grammars over a one-letter alphabet generate only regular languages, or can a conjunctive grammar generate a nonregular unary language? A conjunctive grammar is a context-free grammar extended with explicit conjunction in rule bodies, without the explicit negation operation available in Boolean grammars.

Are all languages generated by Boolean grammars contained in deterministic time DTIME(n^(3-epsilon)) for some positive epsilon, thereby improving the known cubic-time recognition bound for Boolean grammars?

Are all languages generated by Boolean grammars contained in deterministic space DSPACE(n^(1-epsilon)) for some positive epsilon, thereby improving the known linear-space upper bound for recognizing Boolean grammar languages?

Does every Boolean grammar have an equivalent Boolean grammar in Greibach normal form that generates the same language? For Boolean grammars in this setting, Greibach normal form means that each non-epsilon rule has one leading terminal a shared by all positive and negative conjuncts, with rules of the form A -> a alpha_1 & ... & a alpha_m & not a beta_1 & ... & not a beta_n, where m+n >= 1 and the alpha_i and beta_i are strings over terminals and nonterminals.

Is the class of languages generated by conjunctive grammars closed under complementation? Equivalently, for every conjunctive grammar G over a fixed alphabet, is the complement of the language L(G) also generated by some conjunctive grammar?

Does there exist a language that is inherently ambiguous with respect to Boolean grammars? In this context, a language is inherently ambiguous if every Boolean grammar generating it is ambiguous: either more than one rule for a nonterminal can apply to the same string under the positive and negative conjunct conditions, or a conjunct can decompose the same string into component factors in more than one valid way.

Does the hierarchy of Boolean LL(k) grammar languages collapse at a finite lookahead length? More precisely, is there a number k0 > 0 such that, for every k >= k0, Boolean LL(k) grammars generate exactly the same family of languages as Boolean LL(k0) grammars? A Boolean LL(k) grammar is a Boolean grammar satisfying a uniqueness condition for generalized recursive-descent parsing with k-symbol lookahead: for each nonterminal, lookahead string of length at most k, and possible surrounding sequence of conjuncts, at most one rule can apply.

Does the hierarchy of Boolean grammars by number of nonterminal symbols collapse? That is, is there a fixed number k > 0 such that every language generated by any Boolean grammar can also be generated by a Boolean grammar with at most k nonterminals?

trace.notes: Normalized the input as a zbMATH URL. The zbMATH API record identified Zbl 1169.68454, Alexander Okhotin, Bull. EATCS 91, pages 96-119, 2007, with the title used here.

The zbMATH web page was blocked by a Cloudflare challenge. Exact-title recovery found an archived TUCS record for Technical Report 794 with the same title and full-text PDF TR794.pdf, which was downloaded for extraction.

Mapped the PDF as title and abstract, Section 1 Introduction, Section 2 Definitions, Section 2.4 comparison of language families, Section 3 with nine numbered problem subsections, Section 4 conclusion and award announcement, and references. The likely open-problem regions are Section 3.1 through Section 3.9 on PDF pages 17-24.

Extracted the numbered problem in Section 3.4 about space complexity for Boolean grammar languages.
Extracted the numbered problem in Section 3.5 about Greibach normal form for Boolean grammars.

Extracted the numbered problem in Section 3.7 about inherent ambiguity for Boolean grammars.
Extracted the numbered problem in Section 3.8 about the Boolean LL(k) hierarchy.
Extracted the numbered problem in Section 3.9 about nonterminal complexity of Boolean grammars.
Expanded the compressed problem statement with the supported Boolean grammar setting and the deterministic time-bounded linear-bounded-automaton comparison class.
Expanded the unary-alphabet question with the supported distinction between conjunctive grammars and Boolean grammars.
Restated the time-complexity question as an improvement over the known cubic recognition bound discussed in Section 3.3.
Restated the space-complexity question as an improvement over the known linear-space recognition bound discussed in Section 3.4.
Expanded Greibach normal form using the rule shape introduced immediately before the problem statement.
Expanded closure under complementation into the equivalent grammar-existence formulation for complements.
Expanded inherent ambiguity using the two ambiguity modes defined at the start of Section 3.7.
Expanded the Boolean LL(k) hierarchy question with the finite-collapse formulation and a concise version of the k-lookahead uniqueness condition.
Expanded the nonterminal-complexity question into the fixed-k collapse formulation.
No near-duplicates were merged; the nine numbered problems address distinct research questions.
